Cheat sheet

CRES Memorization Sheet

Print this and keep it beside you. The CRES exam rewards recall of dose limits, the inverse square law, tube and generator relationships, QC tolerances, regulators and what each asks for, and the network tools of the imaging department. Every number on this sheet is fair game.

01The exam itself

FactValue
Certifying bodyAAMI Credentials Institute (ACI), the credentialing arm of AAMI
Questions and time165 multiple-choice questions in 3 hours, closed book; on-screen calculator and notepad only
Delivery and windowsComputer-based at Kryterion centers, travel up to 100 miles; twice a year, May 1 to 15 and November 1 to 15
The six domainsAnatomy and Physiology 7 percent; Public Safety in the Healthcare Facility 8; Fundamentals of Electricity and Electronics 10; Healthcare Technology and Function 25; Healthcare Technology Problem Solving 25; Healthcare Information Technology 25
PassingA criterion-referenced cut score set by the modified Angoff method; no cut score is published
ResultsPass or fail on screen and by email within 24 hours; those who do not pass also get a scaled score and an analysis of performance
Fee$410 member, $460 non-member; retake $355 member, $405 non-member
Retakes and recertification60 days between attempts, three attempts in two years, then a one-year wait; recertify every three years with continuing education
Where the points areFunction, problem solving, and informatics are 75 percent; the first three domains are 25 percent
Eligibility pathwayWhat it requires
Pathway 1, educationAn associate degree or higher in an electronics, technology, or science program plus two years of full-time BMET work
Pathway 2, militaryA United States military biomedical equipment technology program plus two years of full-time BMET work
Pathway 3, experienceFour years of full-time BMET work
Radiology specialty clauseFull certification also requires at least 40 percent of work experience in the radiology specialty over the last two years, with 25 percent over the last five years
Candidate statusThe degree alone, the military program alone, or two years of work alone earns candidate status, not full certification
Credential ladderCABT entry associate, CBET general technician, CRES imaging specialist, CHTM manager; all four are ACI credentials inside HTM
This course's official-format test uses 70%, the same bar as our CBET course; ACI publishes no cut score.

02Anatomy, positioning, and terminology

Direction or position termsPlain meaning
Anterior (ventral), posterior (dorsal)Toward the front; toward the back
Superior, inferiorToward the head; toward the feet
Medial, lateralToward the midline; away from it
Proximal, distalNearer the trunk or attachment; farther from it
Supine, prone, erect, recumbentFace up; face down; upright; lying down in any position
Lateral decubitusOn a side, horizontal beam; right or left names the down side
Dorsal and ventral decubitusOn the back, or face down, horizontal beam crossing side to side
Projection or positionBeam path and equipment
APEnters the front, exits the back; patient supine or erect facing the tube
PAEnters the back, exits the front; patient faces the receptor, so less magnification
LateralCrosses side to side; the named side is against the receptor
Oblique: RAO, LAO, RPO, LPOBody rotated between frontal and lateral, tube and receptor square. RAO right front to the receptor, LAO left front, RPO right back, LPO left back
Axial, tangentialAlong the long axis of the part; or skimming a surface to clear other anatomy
DecubitusLying down with a horizontal beam, so air and fluid levels show
Plane, line, or landmarkHow it divides, or where it runs
Sagittal, median (midsagittal)Vertically into left and right; the median plane into equal halves
MidcoronalVertically into anterior and posterior parts
Transverse (axial)Horizontally into superior and inferior parts; state the level
Orbitomeatal, infraorbitomeatalOuter canthus of the eye, or just below the eye, to the auricular point (ear canal)
Glabellomeatal, acanthiomeatalThe glabella between the eyebrows, or the acanthion where nose meets upper lip, to the auricular point
T1About 2 inches above the sternal notch
T2 to T3, then T4 to T5 disc spacesThe sternal notch at the jugular; then the sternal angle
T6 to T7 disc space, then T10The lower end of the scapula; then the xiphoid tip
Column count33 bones: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, coccyx of 4 fused
Body habitusShareWhere the organs sit
HypersthenicAbout 5 percentMassive, broad deep midsection, ribs nearly parallel to the floor; high diaphragm, short wide heart, high transverse medial stomach, high outside gallbladder, colon framing the abdomen; most exposure
SthenicAbout 50 percentThe average athletic build technique charts are based on; ribs sloping down, stomach high and left, colon evenly spread, gallbladder centered right
HyposthenicAbout 35 percentMore slender than sthenic; stomach and gallbladder high; less exposure
AsthenicAbout 10 percentFrail and slim, long shallow narrow midsection; heart nearly vertical at the midline, low medial stomach, low midline gallbladder, low colon; least exposure
Why it matters6 to 8 inchesHabitus shifts the diaphragm, stomach, gallbladder, heart, and lungs that far, so centering and collimation change with build
SystemKey organsWhat imaging showsOne pathology
CirculatoryHeart, arteries, veins, capillariesAngiographic and interventional runs; heart size on a chest imageArterial stenosis
RespiratoryTrachea, bronchi, lungs, diaphragm, pleuraChest radiography: air, fluid, lung markingsPneumonia, pneumothorax
GastrointestinalEsophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, gallbladder, pancreasContrast swallows and enemas, abdominal series, fluoroscopy of motionObstruction, ulcer
UrinaryKidneys, ureters, bladder, urethraContrast studies of the collecting systemStones
MusculoskeletalBones, joints, muscles, tendonsMost plain-film work: alignment, cortex, joint spacesFracture, arthritis
NervousBrain, spinal cord, peripheral nervesSkull and spine positioning; cross-sectional for soft tissueDisc herniation, bleed
EndocrineThyroid, parathyroid, adrenals, pancreas, pituitaryThyroid uptake work, neck soft tissueThyroid nodule
LymphaticNodes, spleen, thymus, tonsilsNode chains and spleen on cross-sectional workEnlarged nodes

Word parts and the abdominal map

  • Prefixes: brady- slow, tachy- fast, hyper- above normal, hypo- below normal, a- or an- without, dys- difficult, peri- around, endo- inside, retro- behind, sub- under
  • Roots: cardi heart, pulmo or pneumo lung, nephro or reno kidney, hepat liver, gastro stomach, entero intestine, osteo bone, arthro joint, encephal brain, mammo breast, angio vessel
  • Suffixes: -itis inflammation, -ectomy removal, -ostomy opening, -oscopy viewing, -graphy recording, -gram the record, -algia pain, -megaly enlargement, -oma tumor, -osis condition
  • Map: the median and a transverse plane cross at the navel to give four quadrants; anatomically there are nine regions (hypochondrium, epigastrium, lumbar, umbilical, iliac, hypogastrium)
  • Requisition words: bilateral both sides, unilateral one, ipsilateral same side, contralateral opposite, portable at the bedside, stat now

03Radiation: quantities, limits, and protection

QuantityUnit and conversion
Exposure and air kermaRoentgen (R), and 1 R = 2.58 x 10 to the minus 4 C/kg in SI units; air kerma in gray (Gy) is the SI replacement
Absorbed doseGray (Gy), or rad; 1 Gy = 100 rad
Equivalent doseSievert (Sv), or rem; 1 Sv = 100 rem
Effective doseSievert, weighted for radiation type and tissue sensitivity
Prefixesmilli a thousandth (mSv, mGy, mR), micro a millionth; 1 mSv = 1000 microsieverts
Dose limit (annual unless stated)Value
Occupational effective dose50 mSv per year, and a cumulative limit of 10 mSv x age in years
Occupational organ limitsLens of the eye 150 mSv per year; thyroid, skin, hands, and feet 500 mSv per year
Public1 mSv per year frequent exposure, 5 mSv infrequent
Embryo or fetus5 mSv over the gestation; 0.5 mSv in any month once declared
Education and training, under 181 mSv per year
Natural backgroundAbout 3 mSv per year, radon the largest part; one chest image about 0.02 mSv
Cardinal rule or lawWhat it says
Time, distance, shieldingDose rises with beam-on time; distance is the strongest control, so one step back beats any apron; shielding is aprons, mobile shields, the booth barrier, and lead in the walls
Inverse square lawI1 / I2 = (d2 / d1) squared. Double the distance, one quarter the intensity. Halving a fluoroscope's skin distance from 40 cm to 20 cm raises entrance exposure about four times
ALARAAs low as reasonably achievable: lowest technique, smallest field, fewest exposures
Protective apparel and barrierSpecification
Aprons and gloves0.25, 0.5, and 1 mm lead equivalent; at least 0.25 mm Pb required, 0.5 mm Pb normal. At 75 kVp, 0.25 mm Pb attenuates about 66 percent and 1 mm Pb about 99 percent, but 1 mm can weigh 12 kg (25 lb)
Thyroid and gonadal shieldsUsed and inspected like an apron; read the lead equivalent marked on the garment
Inspection and retirementFluoroscope or radiograph every apron, glove, and shield at least yearly, or use 120 kVp at 10 mAs radiography; replace on cracks, tears, or holes; store on racks
Gonadal shielding practiceCuts ovary dose about 50 percent, testicular about 95 percent; use within about 0.5 cm of the primary beam. Flat contact shields lie on the patient, shadow shields hang in the beam
Bucky slot cover and curtainEach at least 0.25 mm Pb equivalent; the cover closes the roughly 5 cm gap at gonadal level
Barriers and mobile workThe fluoroscopic receptor assembly is a primary barrier of at least 2 mm Pb, interlocked so the tube cannot energize parked; the booth is about 1/16 inch lead equivalent; a mobile switch must reach 2 m from the tube
Fluoroscopy limitValue
Tabletop intensityNot above 10 R/min (100 mGy/min) without high-level control, 20 R/min (200 mGy/min) with it, and not above 2.1 R/min (21 mGy/min) per mA at 80 kVp. No limit while recording
Cumulative timerAudible signal at 5 minutes of beam-on time; record beam-on time every exam
Minimum source-to-skin distance (SSD)Not less than 38 cm stationary, not less than 30 cm mobile
Control, filtration, collimationDead-man control stops the beam on release; total filtration at least 2.5 mm Al equivalent; an unexposed border must show with the input phosphor 35 cm above the tabletop
MRI safety itemWhat to know
ZonesZone I public, Zone II reception and screening, Zone III controlled and badged, Zone IV the magnet room
Field and the 5-gauss line1 T = 10,000 gauss, a common magnet is 3 T, the field is never off. The posted 5-gauss line marks where an implant or pacemaker can be disturbed, so screening happens before it
Projectiles and screeningAny ferromagnetic tool, cylinder, or cart becomes a missile; screen every person and item every time. Labels are MR Safe, MR Conditional, or MR Unsafe
Quench and cryogensLoss of superconduction boils off the cryogen; the quench pipe vents outside, a room-side release displaces oxygen. Liquid helium boils at 4 K, nitrogen at 77 K
RF energy and EMIDeposited RF heats tissue, so looped leads and damaged coils cause burns. The scanner also interferes with nearby monitors and pumps, and a noisy device spoils the image
Pregnancy and pediatrics: ask, then declare. Once declared, the 0.5 mSv monthly limit applies to the embryo or fetus. Shield what is not being imaged, collimate to the anatomy, use the lowest technique that answers the question, immobilize rather than repeat, and use a gonadal shield whenever it will not cover the region of interest. Children are more radiosensitive because dividing cells are the most sensitive cells there are.

04Regulators, standards, and what each asks for

BodyWhat it does and what it asks you for
FDARegulates devices and radiation-emitting products through CDRH, which carries the work the former BRH began; publishes the standards in 21 CFR 1020 and runs recalls and device reporting
State radiation control programsRegister every tube, inspect rooms, set operator and posting rules; CRCPD is where those programs write their shared suggested regulations
NRCLicenses byproduct radioactive material, so nuclear medicine carries its own license, surveys, and records
CMS and TJCCMS sets the conditions of participation and may survey directly; The Joint Commission surveys environment of care, asking for the inventory, maintenance strategy, PM completion, test records, and inspection history
MQSA and ACRFederal mammography law under the FDA: accreditation, annual inspection, an annual medical physicist survey, personnel qualifications, a written QC program. ACR accredits facilities and publishes the phantoms
OSHAWorker safety: hazard communication, bloodborne pathogens, electrical practice, and the PPE the employer must supply
ANSI and AAMIThe equipment-management standards a technology program is written against; ANSI accredits the process, AAMI writes the content
NCRP and NEMANCRP publishes the dose limits and shielding reports barriers are designed from; NEMA carries manufacturer standards such as focal spot tolerances
Federal performance numberLimit
Tube housing leakage radiationLess than 100 mR/h (about 1 mGy/h) at 1 m from the housing
AEC backup timerMust end the exposure at 6 s or 600 mAs, whichever comes first
Light field to x-ray fieldWithin 2 percent of the SID; at a 100 cm SID that is 2 cm
Console and geometry indicatorsPBL within 2 percent of the SID, the SID indicator within 2 percent, and the console must show exposure conditions and that the tube is energized
Minimum total filtrationAt least 2.5 mm Al above 70 kVp, 1.5 mm Al from 50 to 70 kVp, 0.5 mm Al below 50 kVp
Minimum HVL (mm Al) by waveform30 kVp50 kVp70 kVp90 kVp130 kVp
Single phase0.31.21.62.63.6
Three phase or high frequency0.41.52.03.14.2
CMMS recordWhat it must hold
Equipment inventoryEvery device by control number, model, serial number, location, risk class, and interval; the first thing a surveyor asks for
Work orderWho, what, when, the symptom in the caller's words, the finding, parts, labor, and readings after the repair
PM due listWhat is due, what is overdue, and the completion rate by area
Service history and recallsEvery visit on a device, vendor reports included, so repeat failures show; plus which devices a notice touches and what was done
Compliance and performance reportsPM completion, failures, downtime, and cost per device for management review

05Electricity, electronics, and imaging power

FormulaStatement
Ohm's lawV = I x R; I = V / R; R = V / I
PowerP = V x I; P = I squared x R; P = V squared / R, in watts
Series and parallelSeries: one path, resistances add, same current, voltages add. Parallel: several paths, reciprocals add, same voltage, branch currents add
Imaging system power rating(mA x kVp) / 1000 = kW, so 1,000 mA at 120 kVp is 120 kW; multiply by 0.7 single phase
Transformer turns and AC valuesSecondary voltage = primary voltage x turns ratio, so 120 V at 750:1 gives 90 kVp. RMS = 0.707 x peak, peak = 1.414 x RMS; mains is 120 V RMS at 60 Hz
Prefix or unitMeaning on an imaging console
kilo, milli, microA thousand, a thousandth, a millionth: kV and kW, mA and ms, and the microamps leakage limits use
kVp, mA, and mAsKilovolt peak is the highest voltage across the tube and sets quality; mA is tube current and sets quantity; mAs is mA x exposure time in seconds, the one number that sets how many x-rays are made
ComponentWhat it does in imaging equipment
Resistor, capacitor, inductorA resistor limits current and drops voltage, and sets mA in the filament circuit. A capacitor stores charge, smooths rectified voltage, passes AC and blocks DC. An inductor opposes a change in current: transformers, chokes, stator windings
TransformerChanges AC voltage by turns ratio: autotransformer sets kVp, step-up makes kilovolts, step-down heats the filament
Diode and rectifierA diode conducts one way, about 0.7 V forward drop in silicon; a rectifier set makes the one-way current the tube needs
Transistor and SCRA transistor switches or amplifies on a small control current; an SCR is a gate-triggered AC switch used in primary circuits and rotor drives
Fuse, breaker, relay, contactorFuses and breakers open on overcurrent, and a repeat trip is a fault, not a nuisance; a relay or contactor lets a small coil current switch the rotor or exposure load
Interlock and indicatorsAn interlock sits in series with the exposure circuit: door, rotor ready, receptor parked, collimator, emergency stop. An unlit LED means the lamp or its drive is dead
Facility and room powerFact
Three-phase distributionFacility power distribution for imaging is three-phase, commonly 480 VAC, stepped down to what each room needs; three-phase service feeds the larger generators
Single-phase service120/240 VAC at 60 Hz with a grounded center neutral; most imaging systems are designed for 220 V, some 110 V or 440 V
Dedicated feed, disconnect, groundEach room has its own feeder and a lockable disconnect: tag it before opening a cabinet. A lifted ground gives a leakage failure and image noise at once
Line voltage compensationBuilding power is never steady enough for repeatable exposures; the compensator corrects the supply ahead of the autotransformer
Transformers in the generatorThe autotransformer is a tapped winding the kVp selector picks taps on, read by a pre-reading voltmeter; the step-up secondary carries 500 to 1,000 turns per primary turn; the filament step-down supplies about 4 A or more
Low-voltage railsLogic and interlock boards run on VDC rails from the cabinet supplies; measure each at the test point the manual names before condemning a board
WaveformRipple and what it means
Single phase, half-wave and full-waveHalf-wave passes only the positive half of each cycle, the least efficient; full-wave uses both halves at twice the pulse rate. Ripple is 100 percent either way, and without rectification the negative half-cycle would destroy the tube
Three phase, six pulseAbout 14 percent ripple, so voltage never drops below about 86 percent of peak
Three phase, twelve pulseAbout 4 percent ripple, never below about 96 percent of peak
High frequencyAbout 1 percent ripple, nearly constant voltage: most efficient and now standard. Less ripple means more quantity and quality for the same settings, so one technique is not the same exposure on another generator
Power protectionWhat it is for
UPS typesOnline double conversion always runs the load from the inverter, the cleanest protection for consoles and archives; line-interactive regulates and switches on loss; standby only switches. Batteries age out
Line conditionerRegulates and filters without a battery: cures noise and sag, not a blackout
Isolation and surge protectionAn isolation transformer clears ground loops and noise; surge devices clamp transients. A surge strip is not a UPS
Internal distribution and brownoutsOne feed splits to generator, gantry, table, and computers, so one branch can look like total failure. Low line voltage makes a generator read kVp low, abort exposures, or throw a line-compensation fault
Battery-powered systemsWhat to check
Where they are and what is in themUltrasound carts and portable x-ray units, on sealed lead-acid or lithium-ion packs; never substitute a chemistry the unit was not built for
Charge before useLeave the unit on the charger between cases; a lead-acid pack left discharged sulfates and will not come back
Capacity fadeRun time and exposures per charge fall with age; log them, because the trend is the warning
What a weak pack doesLow or aborted exposures, resets mid-exposure, or a rotor that will not spin; measure the pack under load
Current through the body (60 Hz, hand to hand)Effect
1 mAThreshold of perception (tingle)
5 mAAccepted maximum harmless current
10 to 20 mALet-go threshold: muscles contract and the person cannot release
50 mAPain, possible fainting, respiratory arrest
100 to 300 mAVentricular fibrillation likely
6 A and aboveSustained heart contraction, burns, respiratory paralysis
MicroshockAs little as 10 microamps delivered directly to the heart (through a catheter or pacing wire) can cause fibrillation
IEC 60601-1 limitNormal conditionSingle fault condition
Earth (ground) leakage5 mA10 mA
Touch (enclosure, chassis) current100 microamps500 microamps
Patient leakage, type B and BF, AC100 microamps500 microamps
Patient leakage, type CF, AC10 microamps50 microamps
Patient leakage, DC (all types)10 microamps50 microamps
NFPA 99 and facility factValue
Ground (chassis to plug ground pin) resistance0.5 ohm maximum for patient-care equipment
Chassis (touch) leakage, cord-connected patient-care equipment500 microamps in current editions (older editions used 300 or 100 microamps; know the limit your facility cites)
Patient care vicinityAbout 6 feet (1.8 m) beyond the bed or chair and 7.5 feet (2.3 m) above the floor
GFCI trip4 to 6 mA (nominal 5 mA)
Applied part typesType B touches the body but not the heart; BF is body floating and isolated; CF is cardiac floating, safe for a direct heart connection

06X-ray production, tubes, and generators

Tube partFacts worth memorizing
CathodeA thoriated tungsten filament, 1 to 2 percent thorium, coiled about 1 to 2 cm long and 2 mm across, in a negatively charged focusing cup; two filaments give the small and large spots
AnodeA tungsten-rhenium target disc backed by molybdenum or graphite. Tungsten is chosen for atomic number 74, conductivity close to copper, and a melting point of about 3,400 C
Rotor and statorAn induction motor spins the anode, about 3,400 rpm standard and about 10,000 rpm high-speed; reversing the stator field brakes it
Anode angle and line focusAngles about 5 to 20 deg. Angling shortens a long focal track into a small effective spot, so a 10 mm by 1 mm line becomes about a 1 mm square; smaller angle, smaller spot, stronger heel effect
Heel effectIntensity is lower on the anode side because those x-rays cross more target material; put thick anatomy under the cathode side
Focal spot sizesSmall stations about 0.3 to 0.6 mm, large about 1.0 to 1.2 mm, mammography down to 0.1 mm. Nominal sizes carry a variance, so a nominal 0.3 mm may measure 0.45 mm and pass
Envelope, oil, housingA glass or metal vacuum envelope; tungsten plating glass causes arcing, so metal lasts longer. Oil carries heat to the lead-lined housing, which limits leakage and shock risk
Production factDetail
EfficiencyAbout 1 percent of the electrons' kinetic energy becomes x-rays, about 99 percent heat
Bremsstrahlung and characteristic radiationElectrons braked by the nuclear field emit a continuous spread of energies, the bulk of the beam. An inner-shell vacancy filled from an outer shell instead emits a photon at exactly the difference in binding energies, and only K-shell transitions in tungsten are useful, above its K-shell energy of about 69.5 keV
Exposure factorRule
kVpSets penetrability (quality, measured as the HVL) and contrast; quantity is proportional to kVp squared
mA and timeBoth linear with quantity; short times freeze motion
mAs and reciprocitymAs = mA x seconds, and any pair giving the same product should give the same receptor exposure, which is what the linearity test checks
The 15 percent ruleRaising kVp 15 percent equals doubling the mAs; to hold receptor exposure, raise kVp 15 percent and halve the mAs, accepting lower contrast
FiltrationRemoves low-energy photons that only dose the patient: average energy and HVL rise, quantity falls
Distance and magnificationReceptor exposure falls with the square of the SID. MF = SID / SOD, about 1.1 at a 100 cm SID and 1.05 at 180 cm
Heat factValue
Heat unitsSingle phase HU = kVp x mA x s, so 98 kVp at 120 mAs is 11,760 HU; three phase or high frequency HU = 1.4 x kVp x mA x s, because lower ripple makes more heat. 1 HU = 1.4 joules
Rating and cooling chartsThe rating chart says whether one exposure is safe; anode and housing cooling curves say how long to wait before the next series
How heat leavesRadiation from the anode, conduction into envelope and oil, convection in the oil to the housing, then the room. The anode is hottest for only about 1 to 3 seconds per exposure
Tube failure modeCause and what you see
Filament evaporationTungsten boils off, thins the coil, and plates the envelope; output drifts low, then the filament opens
Anode pitting and meltingRepeated overload roughens the target; output falls and becomes unpredictable across stations
Cracked anodeA cold anode loaded hard cracks or wobbles and fails at once, which is why the warm-up series exists
ArcingTungsten plated inside a glass envelope conducts, so tube current jumps the vacuum and the generator throws an overcurrent or tube-arc fault
Bearing wearHeat into the rotor ruins the bearings: a noisy or slow rotor, then a rotor-fault lockout. Long fluoroscopic runs are hardest on them
OverheatingThe most common cause of early failure. Lowest technique that works, fewest repeats, never exceed the rating chart; a well-used tube gives at least about 50,000 exposures
Generator controlWhat it does
kVp and mA selectorskVp picks autotransformer taps, mA sets filament heating; verify with a meter, not the display, and keep adjacent mA stations within 10 percent
Time and mAsTimer types: synchronous (multiples of 1/60 s), electronic (common and most accurate), mechanical (portables and dental), mAs, and automatic
AEC and backup timerIonization chambers in front of the receptor end the exposure when enough radiation arrives; cell selection and density steps tune it, and the backup must end at 6 s or 600 mAs
Line compensationHolds the supply steady so one technique gives the same exposure all day
Rotor, ready, and interlocksFirst stage spins the anode and heats the filament, and the ready light means the interlock chain is satisfied. A two-stage dead-man switch sits in series with those interlocks, so an open link gives no exposure and no fault code
Image quality factorRaised byLowered by
Density (overall blackening)More mAs, higher kVp, shorter distance, faster receptorLess mAs, lower kVp, longer distance, a grid without compensation; too little exposure also shows as noise
ContrastLower kVp, a grid, collimation, compressionHigher kVp, scatter, fog, a large field
Recorded detailSmall focal spot, long SID, short OID, no motionLarge focal spot, short SID, long OID, motion
DistortionCorrect alignment and centeringAngled parts, off-center anatomy, uneven OID across a thick part
Beam control deviceFacts
Collimator and PBLTwo pairs of lead shutters at right angles plus lamp and mirror, with cones and aperture diaphragms to restrict further. Light field and x-ray field must match within 2 percent of the SID, and positive beam limitation must hold the same 2 percent
Grid ratio, frequency, typesRatio is strip height over gap, usually 4:1 to 16:1; frequency is strips per inch, usually 60 to 150; higher ratio removes more scatter and costs more dose. Linear grids are parallel, focused grids are angled with the labeled side to the tube, crossed grids are two at right angles
Bucky factorThe mAs increase a grid costs, also called the grid conversion factor; it rises with ratio and with kVp. Contrast improvement factors run 1.5 to 2.5
Air gap and compensating filtersA long OID lets scatter miss the receptor instead of using a grid, at the cost of magnification; wedge and trough filters even out a part that changes thickness

07Receptors, fluoroscopy, mammography, CT, ultrasound, nuclear medicine, MRI

ReceptorHow it works and what fails
CR, and the film it replacedA PSP plate stores the latent image, a laser scanner reads the glow, a bright lamp erases it for reuse. Dust and scratches print on every image, an incomplete erase leaves a ghost, a worn plate loses speed. Film vocabulary survives in questions: optical density, screen speed, screen-film contact
DR, indirect and directIndirect panels use a CsI scintillator over an amorphous silicon TFT array; direct panels use amorphous selenium, with no light step
DQE, EI, and DIDetective quantum efficiency is how much of the radiation reaching the detector becomes usable signal, so higher means the same image at less dose. The exposure index reports what the detector received, and the deviation index compares it with the target for that exam
Calibration and careOffset (dark), gain (flat-field), and defective pixel map; skipping them shows as banding, shading, or stuck pixels. Inspect portable panel cases and cables, and handle boards with ESD precautions
Fluoroscopy itemFacts
Image intensifier chainInput phosphor, photocathode, electrostatic focusing lenses, anode, output phosphor; output phosphors about 2.5 or 5 cm, input phosphors 10 to 40 cm
GainsFlux gain is the 50 to 75 light photons each photoelectron makes at the output phosphor; minification gain is the square of input over output diameter; brightness gain = minification gain x flux gain
ABC and magnificationAutomatic brightness control holds brightness by raising mA, kVp, or pulse width as the patient thickens, so dose rate climbs on a large patient. A magnification mode uses less of the phosphor, so dose rate rises again
Flat-panel fluoroscopyA dynamic flat detector instead of an intensifier tube: even brightness, no vignetting or S-distortion
Pulsed mode and last-image holdShort pulses at a chosen rate are the biggest dose saving the operator has; last-image hold freezes the final frame with the beam off
DSAA mask image taken before contrast is subtracted from the contrast run so only vessels remain; any motion ruins it
C-arm and the suiteA mobile or fixed C-arm adds its own collimator, laser aimers, brakes, detents, cables, and foot switches to the PM list
Mammography itemFacts
Targets, filters, techniqueMolybdenum, rhodium, or tungsten targets with matching molybdenum or rhodium filters shift the spectrum into the useful range for soft tissue. About 23 to 28 kVp, with total filtration at least 0.5 mm Al equivalent through a beryllium window
Focal spot and geometryFocal spots down to about 0.1 mm for microcalcifications; the cathode faces the chest wall so the heel effect evens out thicker tissue, at an SID of about 60 to 80 cm
CompressionPower and manual modes must both reach 25 to 40 lb and hold at least 15 seconds, and 40 lb must never be exceeded automatically. Thinner even tissue means less scatter, less motion, a shorter OID, lower dose
Grids and AECGrids of 4:1 or 5:1 at 30 to 50 lines per cm; the AEC detector sits behind the receptor and reads intensity and quality
Digital detectors and DBTTFT arrays with thallium-activated cesium iodide, or a CCD; film-screen still edges them on spatial resolution. Digital breast tomosynthesis sweeps the tube through an arc and reconstructs slices, adding gantry motion and arc calibration to QC
QC scheduleProcessor or detector daily, phantom image weekly, visual checklist monthly, repeat analysis quarterly or every 250 patients, compression at least semiannually, medical physicist survey annually or after a major component change
ACR phantom scoringCount largest to smallest; the minimum to pass accreditation is four fibers, three speck groups, and three masses, and a score must not fall more than 0.5 from the last image
CT itemFacts
Gantry and slip ringTube and detector array rotate together; the slip ring carries power and signals so rotation never stops
Helical scanning and pitchThe couch moves while the gantry turns, tracing a spiral. Pitch is couch travel per rotation over beam width, such as 1.0:1; above 1 the spiral stretches and dose falls, below 1 it overlaps and dose rises
HU scaleHounsfield units run from -1000 to +3000: air -1000, water exactly 0 by continuous calibration, dense bone about +3000. A water-phantom drift is why numbers go wrong
Cooling and reconstructionCT tubes carry huge heat loads, so cooling and the heat-unit budget govern how fast a schedule runs; raw data is reconstructed then windowed for display
What the technician servicesTable motion and alignment, laser lights, slip-ring brushes, detector and air calibrations, chillers and filters, console and reconstruction computers, and the network link
Ultrasound itemFacts
How it worksA probe's piezoelectric elements turn an electrical pulse into sound and the echo back into a voltage; no ionizing radiation
Frequency and depthHigher frequency gives finer detail but less penetration; sound also weakens with depth and is blocked by bone and gas, so gel and window matter
Probe typesLinear for superficial work, curved for abdomen and obstetrics, phased array for cardiac, TEE down the esophagus, plus intracavity probes
DopplerMeasures motion and flow from the frequency shift of the echo; noise and poor contact ruin it first
HLDProbes touching mucous membranes need high-level disinfection between patients; the wrong chemical or a soaked connector destroys a probe
Dropout and serviceA dead element or broken cable wire leaves a dark stripe down the image that does not move with the probe. Service covers probes and connectors, cart power and batteries, display and controls, and the network link
Nuclear medicine itemFacts
Gamma camera chainCollimator, NaI scintillation crystal, light guide, PMT array, position and energy circuits, then the computer
Technetium-99m (Tc-99m)The workhorse tracer; it decays to technetium-99 emitting a 140 keV gamma ray, the window the camera is peaked for
PET and hybridsPositron emitters annihilate with electrons and send out a pair of photons of about 0.51 MeV in opposite directions, and the ring counts coincidences. SPECT/CT and PET/CT add a CT gantry for attenuation correction and anatomy
Instruments and serviceDoses are assayed in a dose calibrator and contamination found with survey meters, both calibrated and logged. The technician handles detectors and collimators, PMT tuning and uniformity, gantry motion, computers and links
MRI itemFacts
MagnetA superconducting coil in a liquid-helium bath, measured in tesla, commonly 3 T, always on
Gradients and RF coilsGradient coils bend the field to encode position and make the banging noise; RF coils transmit and receive the signal
Cold chainCompressor, cold head, and chiller keep the helium cold; a helium level alarm or a warm cold head is an emergency
Shielded room and serviceCopper shielding and a filter panel keep outside RF out, and a propped door shows as zipper artifacts. The technician services chillers and compressors, coils and cables, table motion, rated peripherals, and the console side

08PM, QC, and test equipment

PM areaWhat the visit must cover
MechanicalLocks, brakes, detents, counterweights, cables and chains, bearing play, tube stand and rails, table travel, collision sensors; plus filters, fans, dust, and room temperature, because heat kills generators and detectors
Electrical safetyGround resistance 0.5 ohm maximum and chassis leakage within the limit your facility cites, with an analyzer, at incoming inspection, after repair, and on schedule
InterlocksDoor, rotor ready, receptor parked, collimator, emergency stops: prove each one blocks the exposure
Radiation outputkVp accuracy, timer, linearity, reproducibility, HVL, and leakage on the schedule the state and the manufacturer set
Logs and documentationRead the error log every visit, note firmware versions, record before clearing, patch only on the vendor's validated schedule, and close the work order with the measured value, the tolerance, and pass or fail
Radiographic QC testTolerance
kVp accuracyMeasured kVp within 10 percent of the indicated kVp
Exposure timer accuracyWithin 5 percent of the indicated time above 10 ms; 20 percent at 10 ms or less
Linearity and reproducibilityNo more than 10 percent variation in output per mAs between adjacent mA stations, and no more than plus or minus 5 percent over repeated identical exposures
Collimation and beam alignmentLight field and x-ray field within 2 percent of the SID, with PBL and the SID indicator held to the same 2 percent
HVLMeasure and compare with the minimum for that kVp and waveform; meeting it proves the filtration is adequate
Focal spot sizePinhole camera, star pattern, or slit camera against the nominal size and its variance
AEC performanceConstant density through varying thicknesses of aluminum or acrylic, plus a backup timer test at 6 s or 600 mAs
When to retestAnnually, after major repair to the console or high-voltage generator, and whenever output looks wrong
Fluoroscopy QC testWhat to measure
Tabletop exposure rate and timerA chamber at the tabletop against the 10 R/min and 20 R/min limits, and the audible signal at 5 minutes
GeometrySSD at least 38 cm stationary or 30 cm mobile with the spacer in place, and an unexposed border with the input phosphor 35 cm above the tabletop
Image qualityA resolution and low-contrast phantom at fixed geometry against the baseline on file
Mammography QC scheduleTasks
Daily and weeklyProcessor or detector check and cleanliness daily; phantom image, screen cleanliness, viewing conditions weekly
Monthly and quarterlyVisual checklist monthly; repeat analysis quarterly or every 250 patients
Semiannual and annualCompression force at least semiannually; medical physicist survey annually or after a major component change
Ultrasound QC taskWhat to do
Phantom scanDepth of penetration, resolution, and uniformity at fixed settings against the baseline
Probe, display, and controlsCracks in the lens, kinked cables, bent connector pins, and chemical damage; brightness and contrast against the test pattern, with every control and footswitch working
Test instrumentWhat it is for
Non-invasive kVp meterReads kVp, time, dose, dose rate, and HVL from outside the beam path, and verifies time and mAs independently of the console
Ionization chamber and solid-state detectorThe reference dose and dose-rate detectors for output, fluoroscopic rate, and leakage
DAP meterMeasures dose area product under the collimator, tracking dose and the volume of tissue irradiated
Phantoms, filters, test toolsCalibrated aluminum sheets added until intensity halves give the HVL; plus resolution and contrast phantoms, the beam-alignment tool, pinhole and star patterns, and the mammography and CT accreditation phantoms
Staff dosimetersTLD and OSL badges read by a service, plus direct-reading electronic dosimeters; worn at the collar outside the apron
DMM or DVMVoltage, current, and resistance at the test points the manual names; on continuity an OL reading means the path is open
Electrical safety analyzerGround resistance and leakage against the NFPA 99 and IEC 60601-1 limits, in normal, reversed-polarity, and open-ground conditions
Dose calibratorAssays activity in nuclear medicine before a dose is given, with its own constancy, accuracy, linearity, and geometry tests
What a surveyor asks forWhere it comes from
Inventory and PM recordThe CMMS: complete, current, risk-classified, with completion rates and reasons for anything overdue
QC logsSigned, dated records with readings and tolerances, technologist daily checks included
Physicist and safety reportsAnnual surveys with findings and closure dates, dosimetry reports, committee minutes, shielding designs
Recalls and trainingEach notice with the devices affected and what was done, and who is competent on what, contractors included

09Troubleshooting imaging systems

The method, every time

  • Symptom and history: get it in the user's own words with the exam, the room, and the step where it happens, then ask what changed and read the error log and service history. Not working is not a symptom
  • Isolate: split the chain into power, control, generation, geometry, receptor, and network, and prove which side of each split is good. Measure resistance and continuity only with the equipment OFF and capacitors discharged
  • Verify: after the fix, run the test that would have caught the fault and record the number
  • Device error versus use error: reproduce it yourself. A fault nobody else can reproduce is often workflow or training, and the fix is a demonstration, not a part
  • Repair, replace, or escalate: weigh downtime, parts cost against replacement value, your own calibration ability, and the limits of your service access
  • Exam wording: a problem-solving stem asks for the FIRST step or the MOST likely cause, so pick the check that is safest, simplest, and soonest. Read what the stem says is NOT true; BEST means the complete safe action, while LEAST likely wants the three plausible ones eliminated
PriorityWhy it comes first
Patient and staff safetyStop the exposure, lock out the room, remove the device from service; an unsafe machine never stays in use to protect a schedule
Clinical downtimeA down room reroutes patients; say when it will be back and give radiology a workaround
ComplianceThe repair is not done until the test, the record, and the sign-off are done
ConvenienceCosmetic items wait, but write them down so they are not lost
Radiographic room symptomLikely causes and the first checks
No exposureWith no error code it is an interlock: door, rotor not ready, receptor not parked or wrong size, collimator, emergency stop. Follow the series chain until a contact is open. With a fault code, read the code and the log: tube arc, overcurrent, line voltage, thermal cutout, failed contactor
Output low or highVerify kVp and timer with a meter, check mA linearity and filtration, then the AEC cell and density setting. Burnt-out images point at a timer or AEC failure or calibration lost after a board swap; density differing between stations is a linearity fault
Rotor will not spin or runs noisyStator drive, capacitor, or bearing wear; a noisy rotor with a slow run-up means the tube is near its end
ArtifactsGrid lines mean a stationary grid or a Bucky not moving. Cutoff names the error: upside down fades the edges, off level drops density everywhere, off center drops it at the sides. On digital, stripes mean a stale gain or pixel map, a ghost means an incomplete CR erase, moire means grid frequency beating against detector sampling, repeating marks mean a scored plate
Mechanical drift, drop, collisionLocks and detents out of adjustment, worn cable or counterweight, failed collision sensor; a safety fault, not a comfort item
Fluoroscopy symptomLikely causes and the first checks
Dim or noisy imageABC at its limit, an aging intensifier losing gain, a camera or flat-panel fault, or a very large patient; compare dose rate with the baseline first. Image rotation or edge distortion is intensifier aging, which flat panels do not do
Dose rate too highABC calibration, a magnification mode left engaged, continuous instead of pulsed mode, or a missing filter; measure at the tabletop against the 10 R/min and 20 R/min limits
Mammography symptomLikely causes and the first checks
Compression will not reach or holdPaddle, drive, or force calibration; verify 25 to 40 lb in both modes with a scale and that 40 lb cannot be exceeded automatically
Images too light or dark, or the phantom score fallsAEC detector position, cell selection, or detector calibration; confirm with a phantom image before touching technique. A drop of more than 0.5 means stop and investigate calibration, target and filter selection, compression, or processing
Filter wheel fault or repeating artifactsThe wheel motor, position sensor, or interlock behind a target or filter error; a mark in the same place every image is a detector or plate defect, dust in the beam path, or a damaged paddle
Ultrasound symptomLikely causes and the first checks
Dark stripe down the imageElement dropout or a broken cable conductor; confirm on a phantom, then swap the probe to prove it
Weak or noisy image, or absent DopplerWrong preset, poor contact and gel, lens or connector damage, or a failing channel; try a known good probe first. A dead display or control is cart power, battery, cable, or the panel
Probe damage after cleaningA disinfectant not approved for that probe, soaking past the immersion line, or a soaked connector; retrain and relabel
Portable and C-arm symptomLikely causes and the first checks
Will not expose away from mains, or dies within a shiftBattery capacity under load, charger fault, a charge interlock, or a unit stored discharged; measure the pack under load and log run time
Drive, brakes, or faults that follow movementBrake pads, drive belt, wheel bearings, or dead-man drive switch; faults that follow arm movement are cable flex failures, found with a wiggle test on continuity
Collimator lamp or laser outLamp, timer circuit, or mirror alignment; a dark lamp invites an uncollimated field, so it is a dose issue
The service report is part of the repair: the symptom as reported, what you found, what you did, the parts used, the readings with their tolerances, and the time the room went back into use. Tell radiology what works now, what does not, what to avoid, and when you will be back. When you call the manufacturer, have the model, serial number, software version, exact error text, and readings ready.

10Imaging informatics

Networking itemWhat to know
IP address, subnet mask, gatewayFour numbers 0 to 255 name the device; the mask splits that into network and host, and two devices must share a subnet to talk without a router. The default gateway is the way out, and a wrong one looks like the whole network is down from that device
DHCP and DNSDHCP hands out addresses, and a self-assigned 169.254 address means it could not be reached. DNS turns names into addresses: if the address works and the name does not, it is DNS
Switch versus routerA switch connects devices inside one LAN; a router connects networks and usually carries the access rules
VLANA logical network on shared switches. Imaging gear often sits on its own VLAN, which is why a good cable in the wrong port gets nowhere
LAN, WAN, and wirelessThe LAN is the building and the WAN joins sites, where slow prior retrievals live. Fixed modalities are wired; portables roam, so coverage gaps leave studies stuck in the local queue
Cabling and NICCat 5e for 1 Gbps, Cat 6A for 10 Gbps, 100 m per run, RJ45 connectors, fiber for long runs. No link light on the network card is a layer 1 problem, cable or port
ToolWhat it proves
PING and traceroutePING sends ICMP echoes, and a reply proves the path and host are alive: work outward from own address to gateway to archive by address to archive by name. traceroute shows each router hop and where the path stops, which matters across a WAN before blaming the modality
ipconfig or ifconfigReads the device's own address, mask, gateway, and DNS: the fastest way to spot a bad address
Cable tester, tracer, port lightsProve the pairs end to end and find which jack is which; lights on both ends settle the physical layer
DICOM echoA C-ECHO verifies the association, AE titles, address, and port: the DICOM ping, and the first test when images will not move
DICOM itemWhat to know
Association, AE title, host, portTwo application entities negotiate an association and must agree on who they are and what services they support. Each node answers to a case-sensitive AE title plus address and port, commonly 104 or 11112; a typo here is the most common reason a new room cannot send
SOP classThe service and object pair that says what a node can do, such as store a CT image or query a worklist
C-ECHO and C-STOREVerification, then the push that sends images to the archive. A node that verifies but cannot store usually has a class mismatch, or a disk, license, or permission limit at the receiver
C-FIND and C-MOVEQuery for matching studies, then ask a node to send them somewhere; retrieving priors needs the destination configured on the sending node
MWL and MPPSThe modality worklist query pulls scheduled patients and accession numbers to the console; performed procedure step reports started, completed, or discontinued, which drives status boards and billing
Storage commitment and GSDFStorage commitment is the archive confirming permanent responsibility, which makes local deletion safe; the grayscale standard display function is the calibration curve that makes an image look the same on every reading station
SystemIts job and the path through it
PACS and VNAThe archive plus reading workstations store, retrieve, distribute, and display. A vendor neutral archive holds studies from many systems in a standard form, so a vendor can be replaced without migrating the data again
RISSchedules exams, holds the worklist, tracks status, routes reports
HL7The messaging standard joining those systems: ADT for admit, discharge, and transfer, ORM for orders, ORU for results and reports
Order to reportOrdered in the EMR, scheduled in the RIS, shown on the modality as a worklist entry, images to PACS, read and dictated, report back to the EMR and the EHR clinicians read
Interface engine or brokerTranslates and routes HL7 and DICOM traffic between systems; its queue is where stuck messages pile up
Security itemWhat it means for imaging equipment
HIPAA, HITECH, and PHIHIPAA protects PHI through its privacy, security, and breach rules; HITECH strengthened enforcement, added breach notification, and bound service vendors. Identifiers sit in consoles, caches, dose reports, and service logs, so sanitize or document before a device leaves the building
MDS2The manufacturer disclosure statement for medical device security: what a device stores, how it authenticates, and what it can be patched with
IEC 80001Risk management for IT networks carrying medical devices: the framework behind joint reviews with the IT department
Least privilege and remote accessSeparate service and clinical accounts, no shared logins, vendor access through the hospital VPN with a controlled account, logged and time-limited, never an always-on modem
Patching, segmentation, encryptionPatch only on the vendor's validated schedule; a modality that cannot be patched is segmented onto its own VLAN with only the ports it needs; encrypt anything leaving the building
BackupsArchives and databases backed up and restore-tested; a backup nobody has restored is a hope, not a plan
Imaging applications depend on each other, so the first question is how wide the fault is. One modality that cannot send is a node problem: AE title, address, port, or cable. Every modality losing its worklist at once is upstream, at the RIS or the interface engine. A down archive fails every reading station while the modalities keep scanning into their local queues, so the clock is running on local disk. Escalate with the device, the test you ran, the result, and the time it started.

11Acronyms

Every acronym used in this course, 146 in all.

AcronymStands forMeaning
AAMIAssociation for the Advancement of Medical InstrumentationThe standards body for medical equipment and the sponsor of the technician credentials.
AAPMAmerican Association of Physicists in MedicineThe physicists' professional body, whose task group reports set the display and equipment test patterns a quality control program uses.
ABCAutomatic brightness controlThe fluoroscopic feedback loop that holds image brightness by raising mA, kVp, or pulse width as the patient thickens.
ACAlternating currentMains power that reverses direction, 60 Hz in the United States and 50 Hz in much of the world.
ACIAAMI Credentials InstituteThe body inside AAMI that writes and administers the certification exams.
ACRAmerican College of RadiologyThe body that accredits imaging facilities and publishes the phantoms and scoring that accreditation uses.
ADCAnalog-to-digital converterThe stage that turns a detector's analog charge or voltage into the numbers an imaging computer can work with.
ADTAdmit, discharge, transferThe messages that tell every system who the patient is and where they are.
AEApplication entityA DICOM node, identified by its application entity title, address, and port.
AECAutomatic exposure controlIonization chambers in front of the receptor that end the exposure once enough radiation has arrived.
ALARAAs low as reasonably achievableThe radiation safety principle: the least dose that still answers the clinical question.
ANSIAmerican National Standards InstituteThe United States body that accredits standards developers such as AAMI.
APAnteroposteriorA projection in which the beam enters the front of the body and exits the back.
ARPAddress Resolution ProtocolThe mapping between a logical address and the hardware address of a device on the same local network.
BFBody floating (applied part)An applied part that touches the patient but not the heart, isolated from ground.
BMETBiomedical equipment technicianThe job title for the technician who inspects, maintains, and repairs clinical equipment.
BRHBureau of Radiological HealthThe former federal office whose radiation-emitting product work now sits inside the FDA device center.
C-ECHODICOM verification serviceThe DICOM ping: it proves two nodes can open an association and talk.
C-FINDDICOM query serviceA query that asks another node which studies match given criteria.
C-MOVEDICOM retrieve serviceA request asking a node to send matching studies to a named destination.
C-STOREDICOM storage serviceThe push that sends an image or series from a modality or workstation to another node.
CABTCertified Associate in Biomedical TechnologyThe entry-level credential on the certification ladder, below the technician credential.
CBETCertified Biomedical Equipment TechnicianThe general technician credential, the usual step before specializing in imaging.
CCDCharge-coupled deviceA solid-state sensor that turns light into charge, used in some digital mammography and camera chains.
CDRHCenter for Devices and Radiological HealthThe FDA center that regulates medical devices and radiation-emitting products.
CFCardiac floating (applied part)An applied part isolated well enough for a direct connection to the heart.
CFRCode of Federal RegulationsThe published body of United States federal rules; imaging performance standards sit in title 21, part 1020.
CHTMCertified Healthcare Technology ManagerThe management credential at the top of the technician certification ladder.
CMMSComputerized maintenance management systemThe database of record for the equipment inventory, work orders, and maintenance history.
CMSCenters for Medicare and Medicaid ServicesThe federal agency whose conditions of participation a hospital must meet to be paid.
CPUCentral processing unitThe processor that does the arithmetic of reconstruction and image processing on a console or workstation.
CRComputed radiographyCassette-based digital imaging: a storage phosphor plate is exposed, read by a laser scanner, then erased and reused.
CRCPDConference of Radiation Control Program DirectorsWhere state radiation control programs write their shared suggested regulations.
CRESCertified Radiology Equipment SpecialistThe ACI credential for technicians who service imaging equipment: 165 questions, 3 hours, offered in May and November.
CsICesium iodideThe scintillator that converts x-rays to light in indirect digital detectors and image intensifier inputs.
CTComputed tomographyCross-sectional imaging made by rotating a tube and detector array around the patient and reconstructing slices.
CTDIComputed tomography dose indexThe dose in one slice spread over a defined 10 cm length, so radiation delivered outside the chosen slice is counted.
DAPDose area productDose multiplied by the area of the beam, measured by a meter under the collimator.
DBTDigital breast tomosynthesisMammography that sweeps the tube through an arc and reconstructs thin slices.
DCDirect currentCurrent in one direction only; what an x-ray tube needs across its cathode and anode.
DHCPDynamic Host Configuration ProtocolThe service that hands out addresses automatically; a 169.254 address means it could not be reached.
DIDeviation indexHow far an exposure landed from the target for that exam: the technologist's dose feedback number.
DICOMDigital Imaging and Communications in MedicineThe standard for medical image formats and for the network services that move them.
DLPDose length productThe computed tomography dose index multiplied by the length scanned, so it grows with how much of the patient was covered.
DMMDigital multimeterThe bench meter for voltage, current, and resistance at the test points a service manual names.
DNADeoxyribonucleic acidThe molecule carrying a cell's instructions, and the target that makes ionizing radiation dangerous.
DNSDomain Name SystemTurns names into addresses; if the address works and the name does not, it is this.
DQEDetective quantum efficiencyHow much of the radiation reaching a detector becomes usable signal.
DRDigital radiographyDirect-capture digital imaging: the detector reads out electronically with no plate to carry to a reader.
DSADigital subtraction angiographyA mask image taken before contrast is subtracted from the contrast run so only vessels remain.
DVMDigital voltmeterA meter dedicated to voltage measurement; the pre-reading voltmeter on a console is one.
EHRElectronic health recordThe longitudinal patient record shared across an organization, which the imaging report lands in.
EIExposure indexThe number a digital detector reports to say how much radiation it actually received.
EMIElectromagnetic interferenceUnwanted energy coupling between equipment; it works in both directions in an imaging suite.
EMRElectronic medical recordThe clinical chart inside one organization, where orders begin and reports arrive.
ESDElectrostatic dischargeA static spark that destroys or weakens electronic parts without leaving a mark.
FDAFood and Drug AdministrationThe United States agency that regulates medical devices, including every radiation-emitting imaging system.
GFCIGround fault circuit interrupterA device that opens the circuit on a small imbalance between hot and neutral, tripping at 4 to 6 mA.
GIGastrointestinalThe digestive tract, from mouth and esophagus through stomach and intestines to the rectum and anus.
GSDFGrayscale standard display functionThe DICOM display calibration curve that makes the same image look the same on every monitor.
HIPAAHealth Insurance Portability and Accountability ActThe United States law protecting patient information, with privacy, security, and breach rules.
HITECHHealth Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health ActThe law that strengthened privacy enforcement and added breach notification.
HL7Health Level SevenThe text messaging standard that joins scheduling, chart, and imaging systems.
HLDHigh-level disinfectionThe level of reprocessing required for a probe that touches mucous membranes.
HTMHealthcare technology managementThe department and the discipline that manage clinical equipment across its life.
HUHeat unit, and Hounsfield unitTwo different units with one abbreviation: thermal loading on a tube, and density in a computed tomography image.
HVLHalf-value layerThe thickness of aluminum that cuts beam intensity in half; the practical measure of beam quality.
ICMPInternet Control Message ProtocolThe protocol that carries the echo requests and replies a ping uses.
IDIdentificationA patient identifier, a device identifier, or the photo identification a test center asks to see.
IECInternational Electrotechnical CommissionThe body behind IEC 60601-1, the safety standard for medical electrical equipment.
IPInternet ProtocolThe addressing scheme that identifies every device on a network.
ITInformation technologyThe department that owns the network, servers, and security an imaging department depends on.
kVAKilovolt-ampereA thousand volt-amperes: the apparent power a supply must be able to deliver.
kVpKilovolt peakThe highest voltage across the tube during an exposure; it sets beam quality and strongly affects quantity.
LANLocal area networkThe network inside one building or campus, where modalities and archives usually sit together.
LAOLeft anterior obliqueAn oblique position with the left front of the body against the receptor.
LEDLight-emitting diodeA diode that emits light; the indicator and display backlight of almost every console and panel.
LPOLeft posterior obliqueAn oblique position with the left back of the body against the receptor.
mAMilliampereTube current: the number of electrons crossing from filament to target each second.
MACMedia access control addressThe hardware address built into a network interface, which a switch learns for each of its ports.
mAsMilliampere secondsTube current multiplied by exposure time: the single number that sets how many x-rays are made.
MDS2Manufacturer Disclosure Statement for Medical Device SecurityThe standard form that says what a device stores, how it authenticates, and how it can be patched.
MFMagnification factorImage size divided by object size, equal to the source-to-image distance divided by the source-to-object distance.
MPPSModality performed procedure stepThe DICOM service by which a modality reports that an exam started, finished, or was discontinued.
MQSAMammography Quality Standards ActThe federal law that sets mammography accreditation, inspection, personnel, and quality control requirements.
MRMagnetic resonanceImaging from the magnetic behavior of tissue in a strong field; also the labeling scheme for magnet room safety.
MRIMagnetic resonance imagingA superconducting magnet, gradient coils, and radiofrequency coils; no ionizing radiation and the field is always on.
MTBFMean time between failuresThe average interval between one failure of a device and the next; the headline number of a performance report.
MWLModality worklistThe DICOM query that pulls scheduled patients and accession numbers onto the modality console.
NaISodium iodideThe scintillation crystal in a gamma camera, which flashes light when a gamma ray is absorbed.
NCRPNational Council on Radiation Protection and MeasurementsThe body whose recommended dose limits and shielding reports are adopted into law and used by physicists.
NEMANational Electrical Manufacturers AssociationThe manufacturers' standards association behind focal spot tolerances and the home of the imaging communications standard.
NFPANational Fire Protection AssociationThe source of NFPA 99 for health care facilities and NFPA 70, the national electrical code.
NICNetwork interface cardThe network adapter and its link light, the first physical check in any connection fault.
NRCNuclear Regulatory CommissionThe agency that licenses byproduct radioactive material, which is why nuclear medicine has its own rules.
OIDObject-to-image receptor distanceThe gap between the anatomy and the receptor; the main driver of magnification and blur.
ORMOrder messageThe message type that carries a clinical order from the chart to the scheduling and imaging systems.
ORUObservation result messageThe message type that returns a result or report to the chart.
OSHAOccupational Safety and Health AdministrationThe United States agency for worker safety: hazard communication, bloodborne pathogens, electrical practice, and PPE.
OSLOptically stimulated luminescenceA personal dosimeter type read out by stimulating the detector with light.
PAPosteroanteriorA projection in which the beam enters the back of the body and exits the front.
PACSPicture archiving and communication systemThe archive plus the reading workstations: it stores, retrieves, distributes, and displays images.
PBLPositive beam limitationAutomatic collimation that sizes the shutters to the receptor in use.
PDUPower distribution unitThe panel inside a system that takes the incoming feed and splits it to the subsystems.
PETPositron emission tomographyImaging that counts pairs of photons emitted in opposite directions when a positron annihilates with an electron.
PHIProtected health informationPatient-identifiable information in any form, including what sits in consoles, caches, and service logs.
PINGPacket internet groperThe command that sends echo requests to an address to prove the path and the host are alive.
PMPreventive maintenanceScheduled inspection, testing, and service meant to find problems before a patient or a schedule does.
PMTPhotomultiplier tubeA tube that turns a faint light flash into a measurable electrical pulse.
PPEPersonal protective equipmentThe gowns, gloves, eye protection, and respirators a task requires, plus the lead a radiation task requires.
PSPPhotostimulable phosphorThe storage phosphor in a computed radiography plate that holds a latent image until a laser releases it.
QCQuality controlThe scheduled measurements that prove an imaging system still performs within tolerance.
RAIDRedundant array of independent disksSeveral drives working as one set so the storage survives a drive failure and raises an alert.
RAMRandom access memoryWorking memory, lost at power off, holding the study a workstation is reconstructing or displaying.
RAORight anterior obliqueAn oblique position with the right front of the body against the receptor.
RCResistor-capacitor (circuit)A resistor and a capacitor together, whose time constant is the resistance times the capacitance.
RFRadiofrequencyThe radio part of the spectrum: the transmit and receive energy of magnetic resonance and a common source of interference.
RISRadiology information systemThe department system that schedules exams, holds the worklist, tracks status, and routes reports.
RJ45Eight-position modular connectorThe familiar eight-pin plug on a twisted pair network cable.
RMSRoot mean squareThe effective value of an alternating voltage: 0.707 times the peak.
RPORight posterior obliqueAn oblique position with the right back of the body against the receptor.
RSORadiation safety officerThe person who owns a facility's radiation safety program and can stop unsafe practice.
SCRSilicon controlled rectifierA gate-triggered solid-state switch used to control alternating current power.
SDSSafety data sheetThe standard document for a chemical: its hazards, handling, protective equipment, and first aid.
SIInternational System of UnitsThe metric system the modern radiation units belong to: gray, sievert, and becquerel.
SIDSource-to-image receptor distanceThe distance from focal spot to receptor; standard distances are 100 cm and 180 cm.
SMPTESociety of Motion Picture and Television EngineersThe broadcast engineering body whose test pattern is the long-standing visual check for a diagnostic display.
SODSource-to-object distanceThe distance from focal spot to the anatomy being imaged.
SOPService-object pairThe DICOM pairing of a service with an information object, which says what a node can actually do.
SPECTSingle photon emission computed tomographyNuclear imaging that rotates a gamma camera around the patient to reconstruct slices.
SSDSource-to-skin distanceThe distance from focal spot to the patient's skin; the fluoroscopic minimum is a federal limit.
TcTechnetiumThe element behind technetium-99m, the workhorse tracer of nuclear medicine.
TCPTransmission Control ProtocolThe connection-oriented transport that carries imaging and messaging traffic reliably and in order.
TEETransesophageal echocardiography (probe)An ultrasound probe passed down the esophagus to image the heart from behind it.
TFTThin-film transistorThe transistor array on a flat panel detector that reads out each pixel's charge.
TJCThe Joint CommissionAn accrediting organization that surveys hospitals on behalf of the federal payer.
TLDThermoluminescent dosimeterA personal dosimeter read out by heating the crystal and measuring the light it gives off.
TLSTransport Layer SecurityThe encryption that protects data while it crosses the network, used on interfaces that support it.
UPSUninterruptible power supplyA battery-backed supply that carries a load through a power failure.
USBUniversal serial busThe common port for keyboards, scanners, card readers, and removable media on an imaging console.
VACVolts alternating currentA voltage reading on the alternating supply side of equipment.
VDCVolts direct currentA voltage reading on a direct current rail inside equipment.
VLANVirtual local area networkA logical network carved out of shared switches, often used to separate imaging equipment.
VNAVendor neutral archiveAn archive that stores studies from many systems in a standard form.
VPNVirtual private networkAn encrypted tunnel; the controlled way a vendor reaches equipment from outside.
WANWide area networkThe network joining sites, usually over links leased from a carrier.
